answer_text:
In two dimensions the Riemann tensor is completely determined by the scalar curvature. Using the usual curvature symmetries, in a 2D (pseudo-)Riemannian manifold one has

\[
R_{abcd}=\frac{R}{2}\left(g_{ac}g_{bd}-g_{ad}g_{bc}\right).
\]

Any tensor with the curvature symmetries in 2D must have this same algebraic form. Its Ricci contraction is proportional to the metric, so the only such tensor whose Ricci trace vanishes is the zero tensor. Since the Weyl tensor is defined as the trace-free/conformal part of the Riemann tensor, it is therefore identically zero in two dimensions.

There is a small definitional caveat: the common explicit formula for the Weyl tensor,

\[
C_{abcd}
=
R_{abcd}
-\frac{2}{n-2}\left(g_{a[c}R_{d]b}-g_{b[c}R_{d]a}\right)
+\frac{2R}{(n-1)(n-2)}g_{a[c}g_{d]b},
\]

is valid for \(n>2\) and contains factors of \(1/(n-2)\). Thus, if one defines the Weyl tensor strictly by that formula, the expression is undefined at \(n=2\). Geometrically, however, the Weyl tensor as the trace-free part of the curvature is always zero in two dimensions.

\[
\boxed{\text{In 2D the Weyl tensor is identically }0;\text{ the standard }n>2\text{ formula is singular/undefined, but the geometric Weyl tensor is zero.}}
\]
